summary: In March 2016 Microsoft launched Tay, a chatbot on Twitter that learned from conversations. Within 24 hours of going online it was targeted by a coordinated attack by some users and tweeted offensive content. Microsoft took it offline and apologised on 25 March 2016.

overview.background: Tay was a research chatbot meant to learn conversational language from interactions with users on Twitter.
systems: Abuse filters (Microsoft had prepared for many kinds)
overview.impact: Tay tweeted wildly inappropriate and reprehensible words and images, per Microsoft.
overview.severity: A public failure that ended the launch within days.
overview.gaps: This file uses PCWorld's report of Microsoft's post. It does not give the exact launch date or hours until Tay was pulled.

archNote: Components and relationships come from the cited source where it describes them. Layout and labels are ours.

diagrams.title: Open learning loop meets coordinated abuse
diagrams.caption: Per Microsoft, a coordinated attack by a subset of people exploited a vulnerability. Many believed users asked Tay to repeat phrases.

timeline.e: A coordinated attack by a subset of people exploits a vulnerability.
Peter Lee publishes Microsoft's apology and explanation.
Microsoft says it will bring Tay back only when it can better anticipate malicious intent.

rootCause.trigger: Microsoft had made a critical oversight for this specific attack.
rootCause.underlying: Tay could be pushed to repeat and learn offensive content from a coordinated group.
contributing: Prepared for many kinds of abuse but not this one
A learning loop on a public platform

evidence.label: Microsoft's apology
evidence.note: From Peter Lee's statement as quoted by PCWorld.

evidence.label: The commitment
evidence.body: bring Tay back only when we are confident we can better anticipate malicious intent

diagnose.step: Review what inputs the bot learned from.

fix.safety: Do not relaunch a learning bot without red-team testing and a kill switch.

troubleshoot.scenario: Your public chatbot learns from users and a group begins feeding it abusive content.
troubleshoot.question: What do you do?
hints: What do you tell the public?
troubleshoot.answer: Take it offline, remove harmful output, stop live learning from untrusted input, red-team and apologise.

rootcause.q: What did Microsoft call its error?
options: A critical oversight for this specific attack

design.prompt: Design a chatbot that learns safely in public.
design.answer: Filtered learning, human review, rate limits, monitoring and a kill switch.
